Location: domain-11-process-cycles.md — Advanced 11.A.2 "Fraud typologies in the cycles" (and Case study "The SoD breach process mining found (KA 11.3)")
Issue: The domain teaches fraud detection but supplies no escalation protocol, and the only worked instance models the wrong behaviour. 11.A.2 ends "Red flags a controls professional escalates:" followed by a list — but never states to whom (internal audit, compliance, legal, the audit committee), that the suspect and their line management must not be told, that evidence and system logs must be preserved before any enquiry, or that in some jurisdictions suspicion triggers mandatory external reporting (suspicious-activity, bribery, anti-money-laundering) and attracts whistleblower protection. A file-wide search for "internal audit", "audit committee", "whistleblow", "forensic" returns nothing. Worse, the case study has the line controls function itself audit the 14 same-user raise-and-approve POs and conclude "no fraud is found" — a self-investigation by the function that owns the control, presented as the model response. As written, a candidate following the text could tip off a suspect, contaminate evidence, or breach a reporting duty.
Proposed correction: Add a subsection "What a professional does with a red flag" to 11.A.2: (1) escalate to the named route — internal audit or compliance, with the audit committee as the ultimate recipient where management may be implicated; (2) do not investigate, confront or notify the individual or their manager (tipping off can be an offence and destroys the evidential position); (3) preserve records, system logs and access rights unchanged before any enquiry; (4) hand the matter to those with the mandate — investigation is a forensic/internal-audit function, not the line controls function; (5) note that mandatory external reporting duties and whistleblower protections exist in some jurisdictions and vary, and legal advice governs. Amend the case study so the 14 POs are referred to internal audit and reviewed under its mandate, with the controls function providing the process-mining evidence rather than reaching the "no fraud" conclusion itself.

Location: domain-13-ai-for-project-controls.md — Knowledge Area 13.6 "Governance, ethics, risk & assurance of AI" (13.6.5c model AI-use policy; also Advanced 13.A.2 Model risk management)
Issue: The AI domain of an AI-named credential contains no external-standard anchor of any kind. A full-file search returns zero occurrences of ISO/IEC 42001, ISO/IEC 23894, the NIST AI RMF, the OECD AI Principles, the EU AI Act, or any data-protection regime. The 25,000-word governance KA, the model AI-use policy (13.6.5c, seven clauses) and Advanced 13.A.2 are entirely self-referential: 13.A.2 says model risk management is "a discipline long practised in regulated industries and described here generically" without naming one, and the model policy's scope clause (§1) asserts it "governs the use of artificial-intelligence tools by all staff, contractors and secondees" while containing no legal- or regulatory-compliance clause at all. This is materially misleading by omission for candidates in jurisdictions where AI use is now regulated (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 reached general application on 2 August 2026), and it is inconsistent with the suite: docs/books/registries/EXTERNAL_AUTHORITIES.md records these instruments as relied on by PML-AI, PFL-AI and the law set, and expressly flags that "PCL-AI (docs/bok/) has no STANDARDS.md at all".
Proposed correction: Add a short "External anchors" subsection at the end of KA 13.6 (and a compliance clause to the model policy) naming, with the category wording already fixed in EXTERNAL_AUTHORITIES.md: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 (voluntary international AI management-system standard — certifiable, not law); ISO/IEC 23894:2023 (guidance, not requirements); NIST AI RMF 1.0 (a voluntary, function-based US framework — "not a standard and not a regulation"); the OECD AI Principles (an OECD Council Recommendation — not binding even on adherents); and Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the EU AI Act (binding legislation within the EU only, phased application, general application from 2 August 2026). Add to the model policy a new clause: "Legal and regulatory compliance — AI use must comply with all AI, data-protection, employment and sector regulation applicable in each jurisdiction in which the function operates; where an obligation applies, it overrides this policy." State expressly that naming these instruments is characterisation, not reproduction, and that only the EU AI Act is legislation.

Location: domain-01-foundations.md — Knowledge Area 1.3 → "1.3.1 Obligations and duties"
Issue: Anti-bribery and corruption, sanctions and market conduct are named once, inside a parenthetical list of "statutory duties", and are never operationalised anywhere in Domains 1–8 (a full-corpus grep finds no treatment of bribery, corruption, AML, KYC, sanctions screening, facilitation payments or intermediary due diligence in any of the 16 domains; the PFL-AI external-authorities register likewise contains no anti-bribery, FATF or sanctions authority). This is the highest criminal-liability exposure in the book's own subject matter: infrastructure project development in emerging markets, transacted through local agents, development consultants and JV partners, financed by institutions whose conditions precedent and ongoing covenants routinely include anti-corruption and sanctions representations. KA 1.3 develops conflicts of interest at length (a priced worked example, a case study, a toolkit register) and responsible AI at length, then leaves the one duty whose breach is a criminal offence as a five-word aside. A candidate can pass this Knowledge Area without ever encountering a red flag, a prohibited act, an escalation route or an evidence requirement.
Proposed correction: Add a new topic 1.3.2 (renumbering conflicts to 1.3.3, responsible AI to 1.3.4) — "Financial crime: bribery, sanctions and the money-laundering perimeter" — built to the same standard as the existing 1.3.2. It must state: (a) the prohibited acts in plain terms, including that a facilitation payment is a bribe in most regimes and that ignorance of an intermediary's conduct is not a defence where a failure-to-prevent offence exists; (b) the red flags that oblige a project finance leader to stop — an agent whose fee is success-based and disproportionate, an intermediary introduced by the counterparty, an unexplained offshore payment route, a request to route a payment to a third jurisdiction, a politically exposed person in the ownership chain; (c) the decision rights and escalation trigger — who may approve engaging an intermediary, who must be told on discovery, that escalation is to compliance/counsel and not to the commercial line, and that the leader may not proceed pending clearance; (d) the evidence that must exist — counterparty and beneficial-ownership due diligence, sanctions screening of sponsors, contractors and their supply chain at close and on change of control, the written intermediary justification, the payment-route record; (e) an accurate external anchor characterised as what it is — the OECD Convention on Combating Bribery of Foreign Public Officials (a treaty implemented differently in each signatory's domestic law, not itself law anywhere), FATF Recommendations (an intergovernmental standard, not legislation), ISO 37001 (a voluntary management-system standard, certification to which is not a legal defence) — with the standing caution that the applicable offence, its extraterritorial reach and any adequate-procedures defence are jurisdiction-specific questions for qualified counsel. Add the corresponding entries to STANDARDS.md and registries/EXTERNAL_AUTHORITIES.md.

Location: domain-01-profession.md — Knowledge Area 1.2 → "1.2.2 The obligation set" (and KA 1.4 "Ethics and the responsible use of AI")
Issue: The phrase "conflict of interest" does not occur anywhere in the PML-AI manuscript set (verified across all 16 domain files, GLOSSARY.md and the appendices — zero hits, as are "recuse", "declare an interest", and any competence-limit or confidentiality duty). The obligation set names four directions of duty — sponsor/organisation, team, users/customers, public/third parties — and omits the duties a professional owes qua professional: declaring and managing conflicts of interest, working within competence (and declining or escalating work beyond it), and confidentiality. This is not a niche omission: it leaves the gate-approval, steering-decision, option-scoring, supplier-selection and assurance-independence machinery of Domains 2, 3, 5 and 7 with no rule about who may not decide. Domain 3.3.2 identifies "capture" (the second line assuring its own plan) as the most damaging assurance failure but supplies no declaration or recusal instrument to prevent it, and Toolkit 3.T.3's decision-record fields do not include a declared-interest field. A body of knowledge underpinning a professional designation that never requires a practitioner to declare an interest is not defensible before an accreditation reviewer.
Proposed correction: Add a fifth row to the 1.2.2 obligation table — **Profession / self** | owes: work within competence, confidentiality of entrusted information, declaration of interests, honest representation of credentials | typical conflict: accepting a role or an opinion the leader is not competent or not independent to give — and a short subsection "1.2.2a Interests, competence and confidentiality" operationalising it as a four-step duty: **identify** (a standing question at appointment and at each gate), **declare** (in writing, to the chair, before the item is taken), **record** (a declared-interest field added to the decision record of 3.3.4 and to Toolkit 3.T.3), **abstain** (the interested party takes no part in the decision, and the minute records who decided instead). State the two hard rules: an interest that cannot be managed by abstention requires the role to change, not the record to be silent; and a leader may not sign an opinion, estimate or assessment they are not competent to give — the professional act is to obtain the competence or decline. Cross-reference from KA 1.4 (verification signature), 2.2.3 (scoring panels), 3.2.2 (steering membership), 3.3.2 (assurance independence) and 8.3.2 (reserve draw approval). Confidentiality should be stated as a standing duty here, not only as an AI failure mode at 1.4.2.

Location: domain-16-transition-closeout-benefits.md — "16.1.3 Readiness as a conjunction of conditions", "16.1.4 The go-live decision, hypercare and reversion", "Toolkit 16.T.1 — Transition readiness certificate"
Issue: The readiness model represents *every* go-live condition as a probability and then trades the resulting conjunction against cost of delay. There is no class of mandatory, non-tradeable precondition. The exemplar is a clinical records go-live at 40 clinics, and its seven conditions contain no clinical-safety condition at all (no safety case, no hazard log, no information-governance or data-protection approval) — while the domain's own Industry variations section, 1,140 lines later, states that "a clinical safety case and its hazard log must be closed by clinical governance before transition" and that clinical safety "is not delegable to a project authority". 16.1.4 then prices "go now" at a 49.79 % clean probability as a live option, and Toolkit 16.T.1 — the signed certificate, the operational artefact a reader will actually adopt — has a single row type: condition, owner, assessed probability pᵢ, evidence. A signed readiness certificate that assigns a probability to a statutory or safety approval is professionally indefensible, and the reviewer's eye (16.A.3) carries no invariant that would catch it. Domains 9 and 14 both carry the equivalent boundary statement in-section (9.1.2 "the optimum among compliant options"; 14.4.4 "expected annual loss is the wrong test where the consequence is a statutory penalty, a licence condition, a duty of confidence or harm to a person"); Domain 16 does not, at the one point in the book where the decision is irreversible for users.
Proposed correction: Split readiness into two blocks. (1) A **gate block** of binary mandatory preconditions — safety case and hazard log closed, regulatory/licence approval granted, data-protection or privacy assessment signed, statutory notifications made, contractual takeover certificates issued — each recorded met/not-met with the approving authority named, carrying no probability and admitting no economic trade. (2) The probabilistic conjunction ∏pᵢ applied only to the remaining discretionary conditions. In 16.1.3, either add a clinical-safety-case condition to the Meridian set or state explicitly that it sits in the gate block and is therefore not among the seven. In 16.1.4, open the option list with: "The three options exist only once every mandatory precondition in the gate block is met; where one is not, the only option is hold, and the arithmetic below does not apply." Add the gate block to Toolkit 16.T.1 above the probability rows, with a signature line for the external approving authority. Add to 16.A.3: "No mandatory precondition is represented as a probability, and no gate-block item appears in the go/hold economics."

Location: domain-01-foundations-of-accounting.md — "Why this domain exists" (systemic: all of domains 01–07, and 00-conventions.md §9–§10)
Issue: The PCL-AI Professional Laws (/home/user/PCI/docs/books/laws/PCL_AI_LAWS.md — 20 laws — and PCI_FOUNDATIONAL_LAWS.md — 14 laws) are mandatory conduct rules for the credential, each carrying a Rule, decision owner, required evidence, escalation trigger, prohibited practice, AI restriction and verification requirement, and each naming the BoK domain it anchors to. A grep for "PCL-LAW", "PCI-LAW" or "Professional Laws" across the entire bok/ directory returns zero hits: the linkage is one-directional. The Conventions state "This Body of Knowledge *is* the credential framework", so a reader of Domains 1–7 has no way to learn that PCL-LAW-01-01 forbids shifting cost between periods to alter reported performance, that PCL-LAW-05-01 governs change control, that PCL-LAW-06-01 governs earned-value integrity, or that PCL-LAW-07-01 governs commercial traceability — even though those laws are the operative "what must never be done" and "who owns the decision" content the domains lack.
Proposed correction: Add a subsection to 00-conventions.md establishing the Laws as a companion instrument binding on credential holders, with the citation convention (PCL-LAW-DD-NN / PCI-LAW-F-NN); then add a short "Professional Laws engaged by this domain" block at the end of each domain (or a line in each "Domain N summary") listing the anchored law IDs and titles. For Domains 1–7 the mapping already exists in the laws' own anchoring: D1 → PCL-LAW-01-01/-02; D3 → 03-01/-02/-03; D4 → 04-01/-02; D5 → 05-01; D6 → 06-01; D7 → 07-01; plus the foundational set (F-05 evidence, F-07 honesty, F-09 confidentiality, F-11 escalation, F-12 retention) across all seven.

Location: domain-03-budgeting-forecasting.md — "3.5.2 Building a project cash-flow forecast — worked", the *Indirect taxes and withholding in the cash forecast* passage
Issue: The passage asserts, without qualification, that VAT/GST and withholding tax "Neither changes project *cost* (both wash through balance-sheet accounts, Domain 1, KA 1.1)". Stated as a universal, this is wrong in identifiable and common cases: input VAT that is irrecoverable (partially exempt entities, blocked categories, non-registered branches, some cross-border supplies) is a real, unrecoverable project cost, and withholding tax that cannot be credited or is not grossed up under the contract is a real cost to the paying party. This is the only extended tax passage in Domains 1–7 and it carries no jurisdictional caveat and no direction to specialist advice, in a book that is otherwise careful to caveat (contrast 7.2.3's common-law/civil-law note on penalties). A candidate applying the rule as written would omit a genuine cost line from a funding requirement.
Proposed correction: Replace the universal claim with a conditional: recoverable input VAT and creditable withholding are timing-only; IRRECOVERABLE VAT and non-creditable/non-grossed-up withholding are project cost and must be budgeted as such. Add one sentence stating that recoverability, rates, remittance timing and gross-up entitlement are jurisdiction- and contract-specific, that the position must be confirmed with the entity's tax function before the forecast is issued, and that the assumption used must be recorded in the basis of estimate (Toolkit 3.T.1).

Location: domain-05-cost-management.md — "5.4.3 Assessing cost impact and protecting the baseline" (and "5.4.1 Why change control matters")
Issue: Change-control decision rights are asserted but never operationalised, and the domain contradicts itself. 5.4.1 says every change is "approved or rejected" without naming any authority. 5.4.3's AI paragraph states "The professional owns the impact assessment and the approval" — which is professionally wrong and inconsistent with the domain's own Toolkit 5.T.2, whose "Approved by" column correctly shows "Project board" for a management-reserve-funded variation and "PM (within delegation)" for a contingency draw. The controls professional assesses and recommends; a change authority approves. Nowhere is there a delegated-authority threshold structure (what value or type of change each level may approve), a statement of the minimum evidence a change record must carry before it can be approved, or an escalation trigger for a change that exceeds remaining reserve.
Proposed correction: In 5.4.3, replace "owns the impact assessment and the approval" with "owns the impact assessment and the recommendation; the change authority approves". Add a short paragraph defining the change-authority ladder by value/type (PM within delegation for contingency draws against a registered risk; project board for baseline-changing variations and any management-reserve release; sponsor/client where the contract requires), the minimum change-record evidence (originating instruction or trend, full impact assessment including knock-on and schedule effect, funding source, approver identity and date), and the escalation trigger (a change whose cost exceeds the remaining reserve of its funding source escalates before it is approved, not after). Align the Toolkit 5.T.2 column set to this ladder.

Location: domain-06-evm-eac.md — "6.3.3 Selecting a method" and "The governance conversation (government angle)" (recurs at domain-04-performance-variance-reporting.md "4.3.5 The exception report" and domain-02-financial-reporting.md "Executive perspective — Domain 2")
Issue: Domains 1–7 repeatedly place personal accountability on the professional — "the professional owns the assumption", "the human signs off", "reject the to-budget claim", "decision-ready, no spin" — but never once state what the professional must DO when the accountability is contested. There is no duty to escalate, no named escalation route, no dissent-record requirement, and no "must never" list, anywhere in the seven domains. The word "escalation" appears in these domains only as cost escalation (inflation) or as threshold-breach routing. D6's governance conversation correctly assigns the decision to the board yet is silent on what happens if the report is edited before it goes up; 6.A.3's watermelon reporting, 4.2.6 margin fade and D2's "onerous test treated as a year-end formality" all describe exactly the pressure that triggers the duty, and all stop at diagnosis. For a certification body of knowledge this is the most consequential completeness gap in the seven domains.
Proposed correction: Add a short standing passage — one per domain, or a single treatment in Domain 4 cross-referenced from 2, 3, 5, 6 and 7 — covering: the trigger (asked to issue, sign or leave uncorrected a number the professional cannot defend on the evidence); the required act (state the objection in writing with the evidence, before issue); the route (project board → sponsor → the accountable independent function, persisting to the next level if the response is inadequate); the record (what was raised, to whom, when, and the response, retained); and the prohibitions (do not sign, do not permit the analysis to be attributed to you, do not participate in suppression). This is already written as PCI-LAW-F-11 (Duty to Escalate), PCI-LAW-F-07 (Honesty in Reporting and Forecasting) and PCL-LAW-04-02 (Escalation) in /home/user/PCI/docs/books/laws/ — import the substance and cite the law IDs.

Location: domain-06-evm-eac.md — "Advanced 6.A.2 — EVM lite versus formal EVMS" (and "Advanced 6.A.1 — Management reserve and the EVM baseline")
Issue: The EVM flagship domain carries no external-standard anchor anywhere in ~14,700 words. 6.A.2 refers to "formal system guidelines and criteria, documented procedures, independent surveillance, integrated baseline reviews" and 6.A.1 to the over-target baseline as something "large government EVMS programmes" do — both describing named, published instruments without naming them. Appendix C (Standards & frameworks referenced) contains no EVM entry at all. A candidate finishes Domain 6 unable to say what an EVMS is assessed against, or that EVMS "compliance" is a contractual imposition rather than a legal one — precisely the overstatement risk the appendix's category scheme exists to prevent.
Proposed correction: Name the anchors at principle level in 6.A.2 and add them to Appendix C with accurate category tags: ANSI/EIA-748 (industry standard, voluntary in itself, made binding by contract on major US government programmes — the source of the guideline-based compliance language and of the OTB/OTS reprogramming discipline in 6.A.1); ISO 21508 (international standard, guidance, not certifiable); and PMI's practice-standard guidance (professional guidance). One sentence must state that none of these is legislation and that their force on any given project comes from the contract.

Location: domain-07-contracts-commercial.md — "7.1.3 Cost-plus and incentive forms" (and "7.1.4 Target cost and pain/gain")
Issue: Cost-plus (CPFF/CPIF/CPAF), target-cost and reimbursable EPC forms are taught, and the pain/gain and fee arithmetic worked in detail, with no treatment of what makes a cost reimbursable. The terms "allowable cost", "disallowed cost", "open book" and "audit rights" appear nowhere in Domains 5 or 7. Every worked example uses an undefined "actual cost" as the input to fee and pain/gain, when in practice the contract defines allowable/defined cost, excludes categories (contractor default, rectification, corporate overhead, non-productive time), and grants the client open-book inspection and audit rights. The controls professional's core duty on a reimbursable form — coding and segregating cost so it survives the client's audit, and forecasting on allowable cost rather than total cost — is therefore never stated, and a candidate could compute a pain-share on a base that the client would disallow.
Proposed correction: Add a paragraph in 7.1.3 (cross-referenced from 7.1.4 and Domain 5 KA 5.2) defining allowable/defined cost as a contract-defined subset, listing typical exclusions, and stating the two obligations that follow: the cost ledger must be coded so allowable and non-allowable cost are separable at source (Domain 5, KA 5.2.3), and the records must be maintained in an audit-ready state because the client holds inspection/audit rights for a contractually stated period. Add one sentence to worked examples 7.1.3 and 7.1.4b noting that "actual cost" there means audited allowable cost, and add a "Basis of actual cost — allowable cost definition and audit rights" row to Toolkit 7.T.1.

Location: domain-07-contracts-commercial.md — "7.2.2 Variations and claims" (recurs at "7.4.2 Certification and payment" and "Advanced 7.A.6 — When agreement fails: the dispute-resolution ladder")
Issue: KA 7.2/7.4 teach the commercial machinery of claims and payment with the legal layer that decides whether entitlement survives entirely missing. (a) 7.2.2 says a claim "must be notified" but never states that under most standard forms the notice is a CONDITION PRECEDENT — a valid claim served late is extinguished on lateness alone, regardless of merit. The point appears only as an aside in Toolkit 7.T.1's usage note ("entitlement is lost for want of a notice served in time"); it is absent from the teaching topic, the worked example, the key terms and all KA 7.2 MCQs. (b) 7.4.2 presents certification and payment as purely contractual, with no mention of the statutory payment regimes that override contract in many jurisdictions (payment/pay-less notice regimes, prohibitions on pay-when-paid, prompt-payment statutes). (c) Advanced 7.A.6 states "Contracts arrange what happens next as an escalating ladder" and lists adjudication as a contractual rung — affirmatively misleading in the many jurisdictions where adjudication is a statutory right that exists whether or not the contract provides for it, and where the timetable is fixed by statute, not by agreement.
Proposed correction: Add a short topic (e.g. 7.2.6 "Notices, time bars and the statutory overlay") and cross-reference it from 7.4.2 and 7.A.6, stating: (1) many forms make notice a condition precedent, so the controls professional's first act on any potentially compensable event is to diarise and serve the notice — with a worked example of a meritorious claim defeated on time bar, plus one KA 7.2 MCQ testing it; (2) some jurisdictions impose statutory payment mechanics and a statutory right to adjudication that override contrary contract terms, characterised generically as "statutory regimes exist in several jurisdictions; the governing law and the contract must both be checked, and local legal advice obtained" — no clause numbers, consistent with Conventions §9; (3) amend 7.A.6's opening so the ladder is described as set by the contract AND by any applicable statutory regime.

Location: domain-07-contracts-commercial.md — "AI in this KA" block in KA 7.5 (recurs at domain-01-foundations-of-accounting.md KA 1.3 and domain-05-cost-management.md KA 5.2)
Issue: Every "AI in this KA" block in Domains 1–7 states the verification duty ("AI proposes; the professional verifies…") but none states the confidentiality prohibition, even where the AI input is the most sensitive material a controls professional handles. Domain 7's single AI block instructs practitioners to use AI for "extracting terms and variation clauses from contracts… digitising daywork sheets" and analysing claims; Domain 1's KA 1.3 block covers payroll and timesheet accrual data. A grep for "confidential", "privilege", "personal data" or "data protection" across Domains 1–7 returns nothing. Domain 13 states the guardrail as absolute (13.2.5, 13.3.4: "Never paste confidential or personal data into an ungoverned public tool"), but Domains 1–7 never cross-reference it — so the KAs that describe the highest-risk AI inputs (live contracts, claim files under a confidentiality clause or potentially privileged, employee timesheet data) carry capability without the limit.
Proposed correction: Add one clause to each AI block whose described input is confidential, personal or potentially privileged: "…and only in a governed tool — live contracts, claim files and personal data must never be entered into an ungoverned or public tool (13.2.5, 13.3.4; PCI-LAW-F-09)." Priority order: Domain 7 KA 7.5 (contracts/claims — add the additional note that a claim file may attract legal privilege and that legal should confirm before any external tool is used), Domain 1 KA 1.3 (payroll/timesheets), Domain 5 KA 5.2 (supplier and cost-ledger data), Domain 2 KA 2.2 (contract extraction), Domain 4 KA 4.3 (packs containing pre-disclosure numbers).

Location: domain-07-contracts-commercial.md — "Toolkit 7.T.2 — Claim/variation file checklist" (recurs at domain-01-foundations-of-accounting.md "Toolkit 1.T.1 — Month-end close checklist" and "Toolkit 1.T.2 — Accrual pack template")
Issue: Record-retention expectations are absent from all seven domains. The books' toolkits establish evidence and audit-trail discipline well (accrual basis columns, change logs, control-account budget logs, the claim file) but no artefact anywhere states how long any of it must be kept, by whom, or against what. This matters most in Domain 7: the claim file IS the case (7.A.6 says the tribunal "sees only what was recorded at the time"), yet 7.T.2's final item is "File progressed to agreement" with no retention requirement — so a candidate is taught to build the file and never told it must survive the applicable limitation/prescription period and the contract's own record-retention and audit-rights clauses. The same gap runs through Domain 1's close pack (statutory accounting-record retention periods, which vary by jurisdiction) and Domain 6's baseline logs.
Proposed correction: Add a retention line to the toolkits and one sentence to the parent topic in each case: 7.T.2 — "Retention: the complete claim file is retained for the period set by the contract's records/audit clause and by the applicable limitation or prescription period for claims under the governing law, whichever is longer; confirm the period locally, as it varies by jurisdiction and by whether the contract is executed as a deed." 1.T.1/1.T.2 — "Retention: close packs and accrual support are retained per the entity's statutory accounting-record retention period and audit requirements." Toolkit 6.T.1 — baseline change and reserve logs retained for the life of the programme plus the audit period. Cross-reference PCI-LAW-F-12 (Record Retention).

Location: domain-08-pm-lifecycle.md — 8.4.2 "Integrated change control"
Issue: The domain's central control is asserted but never operationalised. 8.4.2 is a single paragraph: it states that changes must be assessed cross-constraint and that "The controls professional runs the impact assessment and maintains the change log" — and stops. It supplies no decision rights (who authorises a change: change control board, project manager, sponsor, client, at what value thresholds), no required content or minimum evidence for a change request, no rule that unapproved change must not be executed, no path for urgent/emergency change and its retrospective ratification, no escalation trigger where a change breaches the baseline or the contract, and no record-retention expectation. Searching the six domains for "change control board", "CCB", "delegated authority", "approval threshold" returns nothing. Toolkit 8.T.1 checks only that the change log is "reconciled"; the Case B example authorises USD 9,600,000 "from programme reserve" with the approver unnamed. The single most audit-exposed process in project controls is therefore taught with no governance mechanics.
Proposed correction: Expand 8.4.2 with: (a) a decision-rights paragraph — the change control board (or named authority) approves, with value/impact thresholds escalating to sponsor, client and board, and the rule that the assessor is never the approver; (b) minimum evidence for a change request — unique ID, originator, cause, the cross-constraint impact assessment (scope, schedule, cost, quality, risk and benefit), options considered, and the funding source; (c) the prohibition that no change is executed before authorisation, with an explicit emergency route that requires ratification at the next board and is logged as such; (d) escalation triggers — any change breaching a baseline tolerance, exceeding contingency, or altering a contractual obligation; (e) retention of the change log and its supporting assessments as part of the project record. Name the approver in the Case B table.

Location: domain-09-agile-adaptive.md — 9.5.4 "Reconciling story points to % complete and IFRS 15" (and MCQ 9.5-C)
Issue: An accounting-policy judgement is assigned to the wrong role and given no jurisdictional frame. The KA closes "The professional owns the forecast, the scope-change transparency and the revenue reconciliation", and MCQ 9.5-C's correct answer has the controls professional "recognise on the appropriate input basis (here cost-to-cost 35 %)". Selecting and applying the measure of progress under IFRS 15 is an accounting-policy judgement owned by finance (the reporting entity's accounting-policy owner / CFO), applied consistently across similar performance obligations and tested by the external auditor; the controls professional supplies and reconciles the measurement inputs and cannot change the recognition basis. The text also never says that story-point percentage is not, on its own, an acceptable measure of progress, and never notes that US-GAAP preparers apply ASC 606 (no occurrence of "ASC 606" or "US GAAP" anywhere in the domain) — so a candidate outside IFRS jurisdictions is left with a rule they cannot apply. Contrast Domain 13 KA 13.5.10, which correctly reserves recognition judgements to a qualified person.
Proposed correction: Rewrite the closing sentence to allocate decision rights: "The controls professional owns the forecast, the scope-change transparency and the reconciliation of the three progress views; the measure of progress used for revenue recognition is an accounting-policy judgement made by finance, applied consistently and subject to external audit — the controls professional supplies and evidences the inputs, and does not select or change the recognition basis." Add a sentence stating that story-point percentage is a proxy that is not itself an acceptable measure of progress and must be reconciled to the entity's chosen input method, and a one-line jurisdictional note that IFRS preparers apply IFRS 15 and US-GAAP preparers the equivalent ASC 606 model. Adjust MCQ 9.5-C's option A and rationale so the professional reconciles and refers the basis to finance rather than recognising.

Location: domain-10-scheduling.md — Advanced 10.A.6 "Delay analysis methods"
Issue: The most legally consequential topic in the domain names no external authority and carries no governing-law caveat. Five delay-analysis families are set out, the text says method choice "decides the answer as much as the facts do" and closes on "choosing the method the tribunal will accept" — yet the recognised sources practitioners and tribunals actually reference (the SCL Delay and Disruption Protocol, 2nd edition — voluntary guidance, not law; AACE Recommended Practice 29R-03) are absent, as is any statement that entitlement outcomes, the treatment of concurrent delay and the ownership of float differ materially by governing law and by contract form. There is no "this is not legal advice; involve legal/claims counsel before a method is adopted or a position is asserted" line. Domain 10 contains no external-standard anchor anywhere (Advanced 10.A.1 deliberately declines to name one for health checks), so this section carries the whole burden and does not.
Proposed correction: Add a closing paragraph to 10.A.6: name the SCL Delay and Disruption Protocol (2nd ed.) and AACE RP 29R-03 as the two most-cited method taxonomies, characterised accurately as voluntary professional guidance that binds nobody unless the contract imports it; state that the contract's governing law determines how concurrency, float ownership and the prospective/retrospective choice are resolved, that positions differ between common-law and civil-law jurisdictions and between standard forms, and that a delay position is a legal position — the analyst supplies the method and the evidence, legal counsel and the contract decide entitlement. Cross-reference Domain 7 KA 7.2.2 and Advanced 7.A.1.

Location: domain-11-process-cycles.md — 11.3.1 "Internal control"
Issue: Internal control is defined in a domain whose subtitle is "the control environment" with no external framework anchor and no jurisdictional statement. The definition — "reasonable assurance over the reliability of reporting, the effectiveness of operations, and compliance" — is verbatim the COSO objectives triad, but COSO is never named anywhere in the file, nor is any auditing standard (e.g. ISA 315) or governance code. Nothing tells the candidate that documented internal control over financial reporting is a statutory obligation only for certain entity types in certain jurisdictions (e.g. management assertion and auditor attestation for SEC registrants under SOX 404) and is voluntary elsewhere, so the reader cannot tell whether "compliance" here means a legal duty or good practice. The same omission runs into Toolkit 11.T.1 (SoD matrix) and 11.T.2 (month-end controls checklist), which present control designs with no source and no scoping statement.
Proposed correction: Add two sentences to 11.3.1: name the COSO Internal Control — Integrated Framework as the most widely used articulation of the objectives and components, characterised as a voluntary framework published by a private-sector body (adoption is the whole of its force; it is not legislation); and add a jurisdictional caveat stating that whether an entity must document, assess and have its internal control over financial reporting attested depends on its jurisdiction, listing status and size, that requirements differ materially between regimes, and that the applicable requirement — not this text — governs. Add a matching source line to Toolkit 11.T.1.

Location: domain-12-risk-management.md — 12.1.2 "ISO 31000 principles" (and MCQ 12.1-D, Key terms — KA 12.1)
Issue: ISO 31000 is characterised as an instrument that can be breached, and the domain contradicts itself about it. 12.1.2 and the Key terms table describe ISO 31000 purely by content ("Principles/process for integrated, proportionate risk management") and never state what kind of instrument it is — a voluntary international standard providing guidance, not requirements, not certifiable, and not law unless a contract or mandate imports it. MCQ 12.1-D then asks "The ISO 31000 principle chiefly breached is", with the rationale confirming that disconnecting risk from the numbers "breaches integration" — compliance framing of voluntary guidance. This directly contradicts MCQ 12.1-B two items earlier, whose rationale rejects the distractor "Breaches ISO 31000 automatically" on the ground that this is "a calibration issue, not an automatic standard breach". Domain 12's summary repeats the content-only framing. This is the exact overstatement the suite's external-reference register exists to prevent.
Proposed correction: Add one sentence to 12.1.2: "ISO 31000 is a voluntary international standard offering guidance rather than requirements; it is not intended for certification and has no force unless an organisation adopts it or a contract or mandate imports it — which is why the discipline below is described as principle-led rather than compliance-led." Update the Key terms row to say the same. Reword MCQ 12.1-D's stem and rationale from "breached" to "departed from" ("The ISO 31000 principle this practice most clearly departs from is …"), restoring consistency with MCQ 12.1-B.

Location: domain-12-risk-management.md — 12.3.3 "Drawing down and re-baselining" (with 12.3.1 and Toolkit 12.T.2)
Issue: Contingency draw-down is described as an arithmetic test with no governance around it. The text establishes that contingency is "under the project manager's control" and management reserve "management-controlled", but never states who authorises an individual draw, at what value it escalates, what evidence must accompany a draw request (the register ID of the materialised risk, evidence that it materialised, substantiation of the amount claimed), that the risk must simultaneously be closed and opened as an issue, or how long the record is kept. Toolkit 12.T.2 makes the "Draw-down record" and "draw-down log" an input to the quarterly review and asks "Does every draw trace to a materialised register risk" — but no section anywhere specifies that record's fields or its approval column, so the review's central question cannot be answered from anything the domain defines. The case study's USD 130,000 draw is made against a "pre-agreed recovery" with no approver named. The result is a control asserted at principle level and left unimplementable.
Proposed correction: Add a "Draw-down governance" paragraph to 12.3.3 specifying: the draw-down request as the controlling artefact (date, register ID of the materialised risk, evidence of materialisation, amount and its substantiation, revised remaining exposure); approval by the project manager within a stated delegated limit and by the sponsor above it, with the requester never the approver; simultaneous closure of the register entry and opening of an issue; mandatory reporting of remaining contingency against remaining exposure in the period report; escalation to management reserve — a re-baselining event requiring the change authority of Domain 5 KA 5.4 — triggered when remaining contingency falls below remaining exposure at the stated P-level; and retention of the draw-down log with the project record. Add the approver and approval-date columns to Toolkit 12.T.1's drawn-contingency treatment.

Location: domain-13-ai-for-project-controls.md — 13.2.5 "Privacy, confidentiality and preparing data" (and 13.6.3; Case study B "The pilot that worked — timesheet narratives")
Issue: Personal data is repeatedly invoked and never governed. 13.2.5 warns "Never paste confidential or personal data into an ungoverned public tool" and 13.6.3 notes "data may cross jurisdictions" — but no data-protection regime is named anywhere in the file, and no obligation is stated: no lawful basis, no privacy notice, no purpose limitation or minimisation, no data-subject rights, no data-protection impact assessment for higher-risk processing, no transfer-mechanism requirement when data crosses borders, and no statement that these duties vary by jurisdiction and by where the data subjects are. The gap becomes concrete in Case study B, where roughly 480,000 employee timesheet narratives a year are used to train and run a classifier whose output drives client invoices — large-scale processing of identifiable employee work records, presented with a cost-benefit calculation and no privacy treatment whatsoever (no notice, no consultation, no retention limit). Domain 8's stakeholder register (8.1.3), which records influence and attitude judgements about named individuals, carries the same silence.
Proposed correction: Extend 13.2.5 from a confidentiality rule into a data-protection rule: before personal data reaches any AI tool, establish the lawful basis and purpose, minimise the fields, confirm the privacy notice covers the use, check whether a data-protection impact assessment is required, and confirm the transfer mechanism if processing crosses borders — stating plainly that these obligations arise under data-protection law that differs by jurisdiction (naming, as an illustrative reference, the GDPR as one such regime), that employee monitoring and workforce-data uses attract additional constraints and in some jurisdictions consultation duties, and that the applicable law governs. Add a two-sentence privacy paragraph to the timesheet pilot and a cross-reference from Domain 8 KA 8.1.3.

Location: domain-01-foundations.md — Knowledge Area 1.3 → "1.3.1 Obligations and duties" (candour about numbers)
Issue: The book states the duty of candour only in the forward direction — how a forecast must be presented when it is first presented — and is silent on the duty that actually arises in practice: what a professional must do when an error is discovered in a number a lender, board, grantor or bidder has already relied on. This is not a hypothetical omission; the book's own material turns on it. Domain 6 Case study B is an entire case about a superseded traffic forecast that survived into a financing model, and it is resolved by the *lenders' auditor* finding it — the text never says what the sponsor's team was obliged to do had they found it themselves, or had it been found after close. Worked example 6.4.3 prices a material model error reaching close purely as an amendment cost, with no professional obligation attached. Nowhere in Domains 1–8 does the phrase "correct the record", "notify the lender" or "duty to correct" appear. The omission is compounded by the absence of any treatment of the sponsor's model and information representations, so a reader is never shown that an uncorrected known error in a base case is capable of being a misrepresentation with contractual consequence, not merely an embarrassment.
Proposed correction: Extend 1.3.1's "candour about numbers" paragraph into a standing rule with the four elements the rest of the book's governance already uses. State: (a) the trigger — a professional who learns that a number already relied on is materially wrong, or was wrong when issued, is obliged to correct it, and the obligation is not discharged by the number having been superseded internally; (b) the decision rights — the correction is owned by the person who signed the original output, the decision to notify externally sits with the accountable principal (sponsor CFO / mandated adviser's engagement partner), and no commercial party may veto a correction that is required; (c) the timing and route — corrected before the next decision that would rely on it, and where the recipient is a lender, through the channel the finance documents specify rather than informally; (d) the record — what was wrong, when it was known, who was told, when, and what the corrected figure is. Add the standing caution that whether a specific non-correction engages a representation, a warranty or an event of default is a question for counsel on the finance documents, and cross-refer forward to Domain 6 Case study B and Domain 13. Add a mirror sentence to Domain 6's "Executive perspective" bullet on model governance.

Location: domain-04-investment-appraisal.md — Knowledge Area 4.3 "Decision contexts" and "Industry variations — Domain 4 → Public-sector appraisal"
Issue: The domain teaches only the sponsor's decision rule. The grantor's decision rule — value for money tested against a public sector comparator, inside a stated affordability envelope — is absent from the entire 16-domain corpus (a grep for "value for money", "public sector comparator" and "affordability" across all sixteen manuscripts returns three unrelated hits). This matters more here than in most books because the corpus's own centre of gravity is PPP and concession finance: Kestrel is a water concession, Domain 7 is built on availability payments and a grantor payment mechanism, Domain 5 turns on consents and grantor approvals, and Domain 12 is transaction structure. A certified professional therefore finishes the book able to compute an NPV, an IRR, an EAV and a PI for a bidder, and with no account of why a bid that is comfortably NPV-positive to the sponsor may nonetheless be rejected — because it fails the grantor's VfM test, or because the availability payment stream does not fit the authority's budget envelope. The single existing bullet handles the social discount rate well and accurately ("prescribed rather than chosen", jurisdiction-specific, read at the date of the appraisal) but stops there.
Proposed correction: Add a topic to KA 4.3 — "The other side of the table: how a public grantor decides" — stating in the book's own words: that a public authority's test is typically whether the concession/PPP route delivers better whole-life value than a conventionally procured alternative, that the comparison is against a constructed counterfactual, and that it is a comparison of risk-adjusted whole-life cost rather than of return; that it is separately constrained by an affordability envelope which is a budget fact and not an appraisal output, so a proposal can pass VfM and still fail affordability; that the discount rate, the risk adjustments and the required sensitivities are set by published guidance rather than by the analyst, and that the guidance differs by jurisdiction and is revised — read at the date of the appraisal, never assumed. State the professional consequence for a bidder: the winning bid is the one that is fundable to the sponsor *and* passes both grantor tests, and a bid team that models only its own NPV has modelled half the decision. Expand the existing industry-variations bullet to point to the new topic. No external guidance document should be reproduced or summarised — name the practice and point to the owning authority, consistent with STANDARDS.md's stated policy.

Location: domain-05-development-bankability.md — "5.2.3 The shareholders' agreement: shares, support and dilution"
Issue: The definition names six things the shareholders' agreement fixes — equity share, funding obligation, liability basis, reserved matters, transfer restrictions, deadlock resolution and default/dilution mechanics — and then develops only the liability basis (excellently: several versus joint-and-several is priced at a 3.25× swing for the smallest holder). Reserved matters, transfer restrictions and deadlock resolution are never mentioned again in this domain or anywhere in the corpus; "reserved matter", "deadlock" and "pre-emption" return zero hits across all sixteen manuscripts. This is the book's largest single gap on the audit's "who owns the decision and who may approve it" question, because the shareholders' agreement is precisely where the SPV's decision rights are allocated: which decisions the board may take alone, which require a supermajority or unanimity (budget approval, additional indebtedness, a variation above a threshold, a change of the business plan, appointment of the operator, entering a related-party contract), how a deadlock on any of them is broken, and what a sponsor can and cannot do with its stake. A 10 % industrial partner whose consent is needed for a budget is a very different counterparty from one whose consent is not, and the text gives no way to tell them apart.
Proposed correction: Extend 5.2.3 with "Control: reserved matters, transfers and deadlock", covering: the typical reserved-matter classes and why each is reserved (anything that changes the risk the minority underwrote — budget, additional debt, business-plan change, related-party contracting, disposal, insolvency filing); the interaction with the finance documents, since several of those matters also require lender consent, so a decision can need two approvals and the sponsor register must show both; transfer restrictions and their bankability role (lock-in through construction, pre-emption, change-of-control consent under the concession, and the fact that lenders' security is over shares that may not be freely transferable); deadlock mechanisms and the point that the choice of mechanism decides who effectively controls the vehicle; and default/dilution mechanics tied back to the funding obligation already priced in the worked example. Add a decision-rights line to Toolkit 5.T.2 ("Sponsor commitment and support schedule") recording, per decision class, who proposes, who approves, whether lender consent is also required, and what happens on deadlock. Retain the section's existing counsel caution and extend it to these terms.

Location: domain-05-development-bankability.md — KA 5.3 "AI in this KA" (identical defect at domain-06 §6.4.4, domain-07 KA 7.1 and KA 7.4 "AI in this KA", domain-08 KA 8.1 "AI in this KA")
Issue: The AI sections are strong on epistemic limits and silent on the data-handling precondition. Domain 1 KA 1.3.3 states the rule once — "Confidentiality travels with the data. Deal information entering an AI tool is a disclosure; it happens only within approved, contracted environments" — and it is never carried into a single Knowledge Area of Domains 2–8, even though those sections actively instruct the practitioner to feed the most confidential material in a transaction into a tool: D5 ("extracting defined terms, tenors, indexation formulae, termination provisions and conditions precedent" from unsigned project documents), D7 ("extracting the payment mechanism" from an offtake contract, and counterparty credit assessment), D8 ("comparing a new estimate's unit rates, quantities and factored allowances against a library of prior estimates and outturns"), D6 (the financing model and term sheet). Two of these carry a risk the book never names at all: the D8 benchmarking use implies processing other clients' or other projects' confidential outturn cost data, which is a confidentiality question and, where the parties compete, potentially a competition-law one; and contract extraction under a project NDA is frequently a permitted-recipient question rather than a tool-quality question. An AI section that describes capability without stating the limit is exactly the defect this audit is asked to find, and here it recurs at every KA.
Proposed correction: Add a one-line data precondition to each "AI in this KA" block, immediately before the "where it must not go" paragraph, in the book's existing voice — e.g. "Before any of this: the material is a confidential project document. It is processed only in an environment approved for that data classification and permitted by the confidentiality undertakings that cover it; establishing that is a precondition of the task, not a review of it." For D8 KA 8.1 add the specific caution that a benchmark library assembled from other projects' or other clients' outturns may be used only where the source engagements permit it, and that anonymisation of a benchmark set that contains a single comparable is not anonymisation. For D7 KA 7.1 and 7.4 add that unsigned drafts and counterparty credit assessments are the highest-classification material in the transaction. Cross-refer each back to Domain 1 KA 1.3.3 and forward to Domain 16.

Location: domain-06-financial-modelling.md — "6.4.3 Model audit, governance and its economics" and "Toolkit 6.T.3 — Model governance register"
Issue: The domain titled "Financial Modelling and Model Governance" describes governance entirely as an internal discipline — version register, input provenance, named owner, change control, golden answers — and never establishes that in a limited-recourse financing the model becomes a contractual object. Missing: that the model agreed at close is a defined term in the finance documents (base case / initial financial model), that it is locked at close, that it may be amended only with the lenders' or agent's consent, that it is the reference against which every subsequent compliance certificate and ratio test is produced, and that the sponsor typically represents that it was prepared in good faith on assumptions believed reasonable. The whole 16-domain corpus contains one passing clause on this (domain-13, "the base-case model agreed and locked"), so the governance KA never tells the reader who may change the model after close or what the consequence of an unconsented change is. Separately, neither 6.4.3 nor Toolkit 6.T.3 states any record-retention expectation: the register captures version, author, reviewer, provenance and audit findings, but not how long the closing model, its audit report, its provenance table and its AI-edit log must be retained, in what form, or by whom — even though these are the artefacts a leader would need to defend a decision years later.
Proposed correction: Add a subsection to 6.4.3 — "The model after close" — stating: the closing model becomes a defined contractual object; the amendment mechanism (who may propose, who must consent, what evidence accompanies a proposed amendment); that the updated/operating model used for covenant certification must reconcile to it and that the reconciliation is itself a deliverable; that the model is the factual basis of a representation and therefore that a discovered error engages the duty to correct (cross-refer Domain 1 KA 1.3.1 and the finding above); and the standing caution that the precise defined term, consent threshold and representation wording are drafting matters for counsel and vary by facility. Add two lines to Toolkit 6.T.3: a **retention** line (closing model, model-audit report, provenance table, change log and AI-edit log retained for the life of the facility plus the applicable limitation period, in a form that opens without the original toolchain, with a named custodian) and an **access-control** line (who may open the authoritative file read-write, and what happens to custody on personnel change).

Location: domain-07-revenue-demand-commercial.md — "7.1.3 Availability payments and the deduction mechanism"
Issue: The section quantifies the deduction mechanism to a high standard (the 1.5× multiplier is shown to cost 1.584 availability points of covenant tolerance) and then omits the entire governance layer that determines whether a deduction is ever actually applied. Nothing is said about: who measures availability and from what system; whether the SPV self-reports or an independent party certifies; what evidence must be retained to defend a disputed month; the dispute route and its escalation (expert determination, and who bears the cost); and — the item with a direct cash consequence the domain otherwise cares about — whether deductions are applied pending resolution, which converts a disputed operational judgment into an immediate coverage-ratio event before anyone has ruled on it. The text tells the reader that caps, cure periods, planned-outage allowances and the treatment of force majeure and offtaker-caused unavailability are "first-order commercial terms, not schedules for the technical adviser", which is right, and then does not tell them who decides any of it. A grep of the domain finds no occurrence of certification, metering, dispute or expert determination in any revenue context.
Proposed correction: Add a subsection "Who measures, who certifies, and what happens while it is disputed" after the worked example, covering: the measurement source and its calibration/audit regime as a bankability condition (a deduction formula is only as good as the metering behind it); the certification chain and whether the offtaker, an independent engineer or the SPV produces the primary record; the retention requirement for the underlying availability data through the dispute-limitation period; the escalation route and who may settle a deduction claim on the SPV's behalf (and the lock that a settlement affecting a covenant ratio is not a purely operational decision); and the cash-timing consequence of a pay-then-argue mechanism, with the standing caution that whether deductions are applied pending resolution, and what remedies attach to a wrongful deduction, are drafting questions for counsel in the governing jurisdiction. Add the corresponding lines to Toolkit 7.T.1 ("Revenue mechanism specification").

Location: domain-09-funding-structure-capital.md — KA 9.4, §9.4.1 "Forms of government support" and §9.4.2 "Grants and concessional tranches"
Issue: The government-support topic quantifies fiscal cost, allocation (G1 vs G2) and grant element to two decimal places but never raises the legality of the support itself. It is not stated that capital grants, concessional loans, guarantees and tax incentives are commonly subject to subsidy-control / State-aid regimes and to international subsidies disciplines; that where support is granted unlawfully it is characteristically recoverable **from the beneficiary, with interest**, which is a project-killing exposure sitting directly on the funding plan the topic is teaching the reader to build; that lenders therefore require legal confirmation of lawful grant as a condition precedent and as a diligence item; or who obtains that confirmation and what evidence must exist. The phrase "state-aid and subsidy-control regimes" appears exactly once in the domain — inside the KA 9.4 "AI in this KA" paragraph as something a model must not opine on — so the concept is flagged as an AI limit but never established as a practitioner obligation. Domain 13's condition-precedent categories (§13.3.1) do not carry it either.
Proposed correction: Add a closing paragraph to §9.4.1: state that every form in the table must be lawfully granted under the applicable subsidy-control régime; that the consequence of unlawful support is typically recovery from the project company with interest, and is therefore a funding-plan risk and not a grantor problem; that the professional requirement is a written legal confirmation of lawful grant (or of completed notification/approval where required), obtained before financial close, listed on the condition-precedent schedule with a named owner and retained with the closing set; and that the applicable régime, its thresholds and its recovery consequences are jurisdiction-specific and change. Cross-reference it into Domain 13 §13.3.1 as a third-party condition category.

Location: domain-10-debt-sizing-covenants.md — KA 10.1 "AI in this KA" and KA 10.2 "AI in this KA"
Issue: These are the only two AI sections across domains 9–16 that state capability and verification without any prohibition. KA 10.1's runs to a single paragraph opening "Model-building and scenario generation are legitimate machine work at this scale" and closes on verification; there is no "Where it must not go" at all — and this is the knowledge area covering debt sizing, the largest single structuring decision in the domain. KA 10.2's names two useful checks and a verification duty but likewise sets no boundary. Every other AI section in the assigned range (including KA 10.3 and KA 10.4 in the same file) uses the three-part earns-its-place / must-not-go / verification structure with explicit prohibitions, so this is both a capability-without-limits defect and an internal inconsistency within one file.
Proposed correction: Rewrite both to the domain's own three-part structure. For KA 10.1 add: no model may adopt a CFADS definition that has not been traced clause by clause to the executed facility (the failure mode the paragraph already identifies should be stated as a prohibition, not only as a verification step); no model may select the sizing ratio, the sculpting target or the target coverage, which are credit judgments owned by the lender and negotiated by the sponsor; and no machine-produced capacity number may be circulated without the Toolkit 10.T.4 sizing-basis statement attached. For KA 10.2 add: no model may certify a covenant compliance position or state a ratio as "the" ratio without the definition source recorded; and no model may resolve a definitional ambiguity where the documents conflict — that is a question for counsel and the agent, not a default. Close both with the standard "AI proposes; the professional verifies, decides and remains accountable."

Location: domain-11-risk-identification-allocation.md — KA 11.3, §11.3.1 "Interest-rate exposure and the hedge ratio" (and §11.3.2 "Currency mismatch")
Issue: Hedging is treated as a pure arithmetic optimisation (hedge ratio, coverage bought per unit of range removed, the 70.0576 % minimum) with no governance whatsoever. The text says facilities "covenant a hedging ratio" — governance asserted but never operationalised. Absent: who owns the hedging decision and who approves it (board hedging policy / treasury mandate / lender-approved hedging strategy letter); the documentation set that must exist (ISDA master, schedule, CSA, confirmations, hedge counterparty accession to the intercreditor deed); the lenders' right to approve hedge counterparty standing and the replacement obligation on downgrade; the absolute prohibition on hedging beyond the scheduled notional profile or for any purpose other than the documented exposure (i.e. speculation, which finance documents routinely prohibit outright); the hedge-accounting consequence (failure to achieve or maintain designation puts mark-to-market movements through profit and loss, which can itself disturb accounting-based covenants and reported net worth) and its jurisdiction/framework dependence; and the evidence a reviewer should be able to find. The domain's own §11.3.1 mentions mark-to-market and counterparty credit as "cautions" only. Contrast §9.1.2, which correctly imposes a hard rule ("No shareholder-loan shield may be modelled without a written tax opinion") — Domain 11 imposes none for a decision of comparable consequence.
Proposed correction: Add a short §11.3.1b "The hedging mandate" before the currency topic, stating: (a) decision rights — the hedging policy and ratio are approved by the SPV board on a mandate agreed with lenders; individual transactions are executed by a named officer within that mandate and no execution may exceed the documented notional or tenor; (b) the prohibition — hedging beyond the amortisation profile, or without an underlying exposure, is speculation and is prohibited by the finance documents; over-hedging on a declining balance is a breach, not merely inefficiency; (c) required documentation and evidence — ISDA master and schedule, CSA if any, confirmations reconciled to the amortisation schedule, hedge counterparty credit approval with issuer-standing and downgrade-replacement terms, and the hedging strategy letter delivered to the agent; (d) escalation — any breach of the covenanted ratio, any counterparty downgrade below the specified standing, and any proposed unwind or restructure of a hedge goes to the board and to the agent before execution; (e) accounting — state that hedge-accounting designation, its documentation requirements and the profit-and-loss consequence of failing it are framework- and jurisdiction-specific and must be confirmed with the reporting accountants before a hedge is transacted.

Location: domain-12-contracts-transaction-structure.md — KA 12.4, §12.4.2 "Change and variation mechanics" and §12.4.3 "The commercial arithmetic of a claim"
Issue: Worked example 12.4.3 builds an expected-recovery model for a claim (probabilities 0.35 / 0.25 / 0.40, settlement ceiling 84.68 % of the disputed sum, breakeven disputed sum 6,901,234) that operates entirely on merits and process economics. It never states the precondition that determines whether the claim has any value at all: under most standard forms, service of a valid notice within a stated period is a **condition precedent to entitlement**, so a claim not notified in time is worth nothing regardless of merit — and the mirror duty runs upstream, where the project company must pass a claim through to the grantor or offtaker within that contract's own (often shorter) notice period or absorb it. Also absent from the body text: contemporaneous records as the evidence base on which quantum is proved; and any named internal owner or internal deadline for identifying a notifiable event and serving or acknowledging a notice. Notice and time bars appear only in the KA's "AI in this KA" paragraph and in Toolkit 12.T.3's header line, so a reader working the arithmetic can generate a defensible-looking expected recovery for a time-barred claim.
Proposed correction: Add a "Notice, records and the back-to-back check" block at the head of §12.4.3, before the worked example: (a) valid and timely notice is typically a condition precedent to entitlement, and where it has been missed the probability set collapses — compute nothing until the notice position is established as a dated fact; (b) the project company's own notice obligations upstream must be checked against the downstream period received, and any gap between them is an uninsured exposure to be identified at contract stage (cross-reference §12.4.2's threshold and approval architecture); (c) contemporaneous records — site records, correspondence, programme updates and cost records — are the evidence on which quantum is proved and must be maintained from the date of the event, not assembled at claim stage; (d) name the owner (the project company's contract manager) and the internal deadline for escalating a potentially notifiable event to that owner and to counsel; and (e) note that whether a time bar operates as a strict condition precedent, and whether it can be relieved, is jurisdiction- and form-specific and is a question for counsel.

Location: domain-15-operations-performance-restructuring.md — KA 15.4, §15.4.1 "What distress is, financially" and §15.4.3 "The enforcement floor and the bargaining range"
Issue: The restructuring and enforcement analysis is presented as an unconstrained commercial negotiation. §15.4.1 defines distress and distinguishes it from insolvency, then hands the practitioner a three-lever framework; §15.4.3 computes an enforcement floor of 91.4291 % and instructs the reader which options are "outside the feasible set". Nowhere in the body text is the reader told (i) that reaching the §15.4.1 diagnostic is itself a trigger to take legal advice and to inform the board, (ii) that on approaching insolvency the SPV directors' duties may shift wholly or partly from shareholders to creditors, with personal exposure for continued trading, continued distributions or preferring one creditor, all of which differ fundamentally by jurisdiction, or (iii) that the enforcement floor assumes an enforcement the law may not permit on those terms — statutory moratoria, court-supervised processes, public-service or concession-continuity requirements, grantor step-in, and preference/clawback of pre-insolvency payments can each move the floor materially. The only legal caveat in the whole KA sits inside "AI in this KA", which is precisely where a practitioner working the arithmetic will not look, and Domain 15 contains one occurrence of "jurisdiction" and one of "counsel" across ~21,400 words covering distributions, waivers, restructuring and handback.
Proposed correction: Insert a short boxed "Professional obligation" paragraph at the end of §15.4.1, before any arithmetic: naming the distress diagnostic as a mandatory escalation trigger to the board and to counsel in the SPV's jurisdiction of incorporation and the governing law of the finance documents; stating that directors' duties, the point at which they shift towards creditors, and the personal consequences of continuing to trade or distribute are jurisdiction-specific and must be advised on before any option is pursued; and requiring that no distribution be made once the sustainable-service test fails without a written confirmation that it remains lawful. Add two sentences to §15.4.3's closing qualifications: that the floor is a model of a *legally available* enforcement, and that whether, how quickly and on what terms security can be enforced — including any moratorium, court process, concession-continuity obligation or clawback of prior payments — is determined by the relevant insolvency régime and must be confirmed before the floor is used as a negotiating boundary.

Location: domain-16-data-automation-responsible-ai.md — §16.4.4 "The AI governance frame" and Toolkit 16.T.3; also domain-13-diligence-financial-close.md — Toolkit 13.T.3 "Close register" and §13.1.5 "The data room and the diligence trail"
Issue: Record-retention expectations are absent from all eight assigned domains. Every toolkit specifies owner, evidence, verifier and date to a high standard, but none states how long the artefact is kept, in what form, by whom, or against what horizon. The omission is most visible where the text itself raises the point and then drops it: §16.4.4 requires an audit trail because it is "what makes an output defensible a year later", but sets no retention period; §16.4.1 correctly identifies processor retention ("whether a service retains inputs, for how long") as a contractual risk to settle before use, yet the organisation's own retention duty for the artefacts it creates is never stated; Toolkit 13.T.3 requires the funds-flow reconciliation to be signed before close day but says nothing about the closing set's retention; and Toolkit 13.T.2's model-audit finding register, which is the primary evidence of what was known at close, has no retention line. For a certification whose artefacts must survive a 25-year facility, a limitation period and a change of personnel, this is a completeness gap rather than a stylistic one.
Proposed correction: Add a retention line to each toolkit in domains 9–16 ("retention: held by [named custodian] for [period], in a form that reproduces the figure from its own trail"), and a short paragraph in §16.4.4 and §13.1.5 stating the rule and its basis: retain for the longest of the applicable limitation period for claims under the relevant documents, the life of the facility plus its tail, and any statutory tax, accounting or regulatory requirement; retain the model version, input data version and attribution alongside the output, not separately; and state explicitly that retention periods, and any personal-data minimisation or deletion obligation that cuts across them, are jurisdiction-specific and must be confirmed rather than assumed.

Location: domain-02-strategy-selection.md — "2.3.3 Sustainability and ESG value"
Issue: Sustainability and ESG are treated purely as an appraisal-valuation question — constraint versus benefit, monetise only where a price exists, whole-life thinking — in seventeen lines. Nothing states that sustainability and social-value claims are, in a growing number of jurisdictions, the subject of mandatory disclosure and third-party assurance regimes, and that overstated or unevidenced environmental claims carry regulatory and litigation exposure distinct from the appraisal error the section describes. There is no jurisdictional caveat (the words "jurisdiction", "disclosure", "assurance" and "greenwashing" do not appear in the section, and "greenwash" appears nowhere in the manuscript set), no evidence requirement for a claimed carbon or social-value benefit, no statement of who owns and who may approve such a claim, and no external anchor — while the surrounding domain is scrupulous about jurisdiction elsewhere (2.2.2's discount rate, the public-sector mandated uplift in Industry variations). As written, a candidate could reasonably conclude that a carbon or social-value benefit is a purely internal estimating judgement.
Proposed correction: Add a third numbered part to 2.3.3, "As a disclosed claim". State that where a benefit is reported externally — in a sustainability report, a bid, a regulatory submission or a financing document — it leaves the appraisal and enters a disclosure regime: the measure needs a stated boundary and method, a named owner, retained evidence sufficient to support external assurance, and approval by whoever signs the disclosure, not by the project. Add the standing caveat in the volume's existing form: which disclosure and assurance obligations apply, to which entities, on what timetable, and with what liability for an unsupported claim, is jurisdiction- and entity-specific and is taken from counsel and the reporting function, not from this book. Add the professional prohibition — a benefit that cannot be evidenced to the standard its intended audience requires is not reported as achieved — and cross-reference Domain 16's benefits-realisation evidence. If an external anchor is to be named, characterise it accurately (voluntary frameworks and mandatory regimes are different things) and add it to STANDARDS.md.

Location: domain-03-governance-decision-rights.md — "3.3.2 Assurance lines"
Issue: The section presents "the three lines" as generic professional vocabulary and asserts specific model claims as fact — that the second line provides independent challenge "while remaining inside management's chain" and that the third line reports "to the audit committee or equivalent". This is the Institute of Internal Auditors' model, a voluntary framework owned by a named body, which the IIA itself materially revised in 2020 (the "Three Lines Model", which dropped the "of defence" framing and its defensive/sequential reading). Presenting a specific, revised, voluntary model anonymously as settled practice both overstates its authority and leaves the reader unable to find the source. It is also inconsistent with the volume's own disclosure rule: STANDARDS.md states that "a standard referenced in a chapter and missing from this register fails the build", and no IIA reference appears among its 22 entries — so a framework is in use without disclosure. The same section supplies the residual-exposure arithmetic that the model is used to justify, which raises rather than lowers the need for accurate attribution.
Proposed correction: Name the model and characterise it accurately in one sentence: an assurance architecture published by the Institute of Internal Auditors, voluntary guidance rather than a standard or a requirement, revised by its owner so that the current formulation is a model of roles rather than sequential lines of defence — described here in this book's own words. Add a second sentence stating that it is one architecture among several and that the applicable assurance structure is set by the organisation's own governance (and, in regulated sectors, by the regulator), so the three-line vocabulary is a lens rather than an obligation. Soften the two asserted structural claims to "typically" and note that reporting lines vary by organisational form (the section's own 3.1.2 material on organisational forms is the natural cross-reference). Add the reference to STANDARDS.md under a new "Assurance and internal audit" heading so the register's completeness rule is satisfied.

Location: domain-03-governance-decision-rights.md — "3.3.4 Auditability and the decision record" and "Toolkit 3.T.3 — Decision record entry and its integrity checks"
Issue: The domain specifies with real precision what a decision record must contain and how to audit it monthly, but nowhere states how long records are kept, who is the custodian, where they live, whether they are tamper-evident or version-controlled, who may access or amend them, or what happens to them at project closure. The whole argument of 3.3.4 is that the record must answer "was it reasonable on what was known at the time?" when examined "in a lessons review, a dispute, an audit or an inquiry" — all of which occur years after the decision — yet no retention expectation is stated anywhere in Domains 1–8. The gap is systemic: 5.4.3 requires that acceptance "evidence is retained" with no period or custodian; 4.3.3's baseline archive, 4.4.3's change log, 7.2.3's audit trail and 8.3.2's reserve-draw protocol all rely on records surviving without saying who guarantees that they do. A record with no custodian and no retention period is the artefact most likely to be missing at the moment it is needed.
