Proposed correction: Add a short closing part to 3.3.4, "Custody and retention": name a custodian role for the decision log, change log, gate packs, baseline archive and acceptance evidence; require records to be held in a system that preserves version and prevents silent amendment (an amended record carries the amendment, the amender and the reason); state the retention period as a governance decision made in advance — set by the longest of the contractual limitation period, the regulatory retention requirement, the benefits-realisation horizon and the organisation's records policy, with the standing caveat that statutory retention periods are jurisdiction- and sector-specific and are taken from the records/legal function; and require an explicit handover of custody at closure so records outlive the temporary organisation (cross-reference Domain 16). Add a retention/custodian line to Toolkit 3.T.3 and to the acceptance-evidence provision at 5.4.3.

Location: domain-06-planning-scheduling-flow.md — "6.4.2 Schedule compression and recovery" (Worked examples 6.4.2, 6.4.2b, 6.4.2c and the Recovery paragraph)
Issue: Compression is priced entirely as cost and rework probability. Overtime, second shifts, night working, crew addition and overlapping installation with commissioning are treated as freely purchasable levers bounded only by a "technical limit" in the cost-slope table. Nothing states that these levers are also bounded by statutory working-time and fatigue-management duties, by safety-case and permit-to-work conditions, and by collective or individual employment agreements; that overlapping two disciplines on the same plant (6.4.2c) is a simultaneous-operations decision that in many sectors requires a separate safety review and approval before it can be bought at any price; or that these constraints vary by jurisdiction and sector. The single acknowledgement — "night-shift error rates are not day-shift error rates" — is framed as a quality consequence to be priced, not as a limit that may forbid the purchase. Given the running utility case and the domain's explicit instruction that a recovery plan states "the decision authority spending them", the omission of the safety approver from that authority set is a professional gap, and the arithmetic as presented could be used to justify a compression a safety regime does not permit.
Proposed correction: Insert a short "What bounds the menu" paragraph before Worked example 6.4.2b. State that each compression lever carries a non-financial ceiling — statutory working-time and rest limits, fatigue-management duties, safety-case and permit conditions, and agreement terms — that these are jurisdiction- and sector-specific and are taken from the safety function, HR and counsel rather than from a cost slope, and that a lever whose ceiling is binding is not available at any price. Add the corresponding decision-rights sentence: on a fast-track or shift-pattern change with a safety consequence, the compression decision requires the named safety approver in addition to the authority spending the money, and the recovery plan (Toolkit 6.T.2) records both. Add a line to Toolkit 6.T.4 ("Compression menu") requiring each priced lever to carry its non-financial ceiling and the approval it needs alongside its cost slope and max weeks.

Location: domain-07-cost-resources-commercial.md — "Knowledge Area 7.2 — The cost baseline, actuals and forecasting" (no "AI in this KA" section between 7.2.3 and "Key terms — KA 7.2")
Issue: KA 7.2 is the only substantive Knowledge Area in Domains 1–8 that carries no AI treatment of any kind — the region 7.2.1–7.2.3 contains no reference to AI, machine computation, automation or tooling. This is the KA covering accruals, actual-cost capture, commitment coverage and baseline integrity, which is precisely where automated accrual estimation, ERP/ledger extraction and rules-based commitment matching now originate, and where an unverified automated accrual silently corrupts every index computed in KA 7.3 — the effect MCQ 7.2-A itself describes (a stepped CPI caused by missing accruals) with no statement of how an automated feed would be verified or who owns it. The same structural gap exists at Domain 8, KA 8.3 ("Responses, reserves and governance"), which has no AI section either, despite 8.3.2's reserve-adequacy recomputation being routine automation. Domains 4 and 5 set the mature pattern ("where it earns its place / where it must not go / verification, concretely"), so the absence reads as an omission rather than a decision.
Proposed correction: Add an "AI in this KA" section to KA 7.2 immediately before "Key terms — KA 7.2", following the Domain 5 three-part pattern. Earns its place: reconciling ledger actuals to the cost report, identifying periods with no accrual posted against evidence of work received, sweeping open purchase orders to compute commitment coverage, and flagging control-account transfers not carried by a change reference. Must not go: determining whether work has been received (a measurement judgement with a named human owner), setting or adjusting an accrual, authorising a control-account transfer, or re-baselining — all of which move money or the measurement basis. Verification, concretely: recompute the AC-plus-accrual total against the ledger, confirm the accrual reversal in the following period (7.2.1's timing invariant), and reproduce commitment coverage by hand for one period. Add the equivalent section to Domain 8 KA 8.3, with the explicit prohibition that no model output may authorise a reserve draw — a draw is an attributable decision under the published protocol (8.3.2).

Location: domain-08-risk-uncertainty-resilience.md — "8.4.3 Crisis leadership"
Issue: Crisis leadership is given twelve lines of posture (stabilise, establish facts, decide with a clock, communicate, protect the team, capture the lesson) with no professional operating content. Missing: who declares a crisis and who stands it down; what authority the leader acquires and does not acquire on declaration (specifically, who may stop work, who may commit unbudgeted funds, and against which reserve); the mandatory external-notification duties that a serious materialised risk frequently triggers — safety regulator, environmental regulator, data-protection authority, insurer notification conditions, client notification clauses in the contract — together with the standing caveat that these are jurisdiction- and sector-specific, statutory rather than discretionary, and to be taken from the regulator and counsel; the requirement to keep a contemporaneous decision log and to preserve evidence from the moment of declaration (which is when records are most often overwritten and most likely to be examined later); and the interaction with 3.3.3's escalation route and 4.4.1's emergency change route. The book elsewhere handles legally sensitive ground carefully (1.4.3, 7.4.2, 8.3.1), which makes the silence here conspicuous: the two running cases are a clinical system and a utility, where a materialised risk is exactly the class of event that carries a notification clock.
Proposed correction: Expand 8.4.3 into a section with three named parts. **Declaration and authority**: who may declare (named role), what the declaration changes (a stated fund, a stated stop-work authority, a standing meeting cadence), and who stands it down — modelled on the emergency change route of Domain 4, KA 4.4.1 so that the two instruments are consistent. **Notification**: a stated duty to establish, before the crisis, which external notifications the project's sector and jurisdiction impose and on what clock (safety, environmental, data protection, listing/market disclosure, insurer, client), recorded as a one-page notification map held with the risk register; with the volume's standing caution that the applicable duties are statutory, jurisdiction-specific, and taken from the regulator and qualified counsel, never from this book. **Record**: a contemporaneous decision log from the moment of declaration (reference, time, decision-maker, information relied on, per 3.3.4), and an instruction to preserve rather than tidy the evidence. Add one worked example pricing the cost of a delayed notification against the cost of an early one, consistent with the escalation-timing arithmetic of Worked example 1.2.2.

Location: domain-09-quality-assurance-improvement.md — "9.3.1 The acceptance decision and nonconformance disposition" and "Toolkit 9.T.2 — Acceptance and disposition record with the self-consistency test"
Issue: Domain 9 contains no record-retention or record-custody treatment of any kind — the words "retention" and "retain" do not appear in the file, and "jurisdiction" appears zero times. This is the domain that creates the evidence on which later disputes, audits, latent-defect claims and regulatory inspections turn: acceptance records with named signatories, concession authorisations, nonconformance dispositions, test and inspection evidence, and the cumulative concession register. 9.3.1 requires that concessions be "counted, not merely recorded" and Toolkit 9.T.2 specifies a rich record, but neither states for how long it is kept, who custodies it, who may authorise disposal, or that in regulated sectors (life sciences, medical devices, aerospace, nuclear, rail) the retention period for quality records is set by the approval regime or by contract and differs by jurisdiction. Domain 16 KA 16.4.4 establishes that contract and technical evidence pays as insurance above a 3.64 % need probability and that retention is "a schedule by class, never a single rule" — but Domain 9 never points to it, so the practitioner who adopts 9.T.2 builds the evidence and inherits no obligation to preserve it.
Proposed correction: Add a short paragraph to 9.3.1, "The record and how long it lives", stating that acceptance records, concession authorisations, disposition decisions and their supporting verification evidence are the primary evidence in any later dispute or audit; that each is assigned a record class with a custodian, a retention period and a disposal authority; that the period is set by the applicable regime and by contract and differs by jurisdiction rather than by the project's convenience, and that nothing in the domain states a legal minimum; and cross-reference Domain 16 KA 16.4.4. Add three fields to Toolkit 9.T.2: record class, custodian, and retention period with the source of the period named.

Location: domain-10-procurement-contracts-supply.md — domain-wide; most acutely "10.3.1 Contract strategy as risk allocation" and "10.4.3 Ethical and sustainable sourcing"
Issue: Domain 10 anchors to no external authority anywhere in ~20,500 words. No standard-form contract family is named (NEC, FIDIC, JCT or their civil-law equivalents), no voluntary standard is cited for procurement or supplier collaboration, and 10.4.3 — a section entirely about human rights, forced labour and supply-chain due diligence — names no international instrument at all, referring only to unspecified "human-rights, modern-slavery or supply-chain due-diligence legislation". The jurisdictional caveats in the domain are exemplary; what is absent is the portable, non-jurisdictional anchor a certification body of knowledge is expected to give, and the omission is inconsistent within the book — Domain 9 anchors ISO 9000/9001 and Domain 14 anchors ISO/IEC 42001, 23894, 27001, 27701, 62443, 8000, 25012, IEC 38507 and ISO 19650. A candidate leaves Domain 10 unable to name a single recognised reference point for contract form, sustainable procurement, collaborative supplier relationships or human-rights due diligence. The same gap exists in Domains 11, 12, 13, 15 and 16, which name no external authority either.
Proposed correction: Add a short "Reference points" paragraph to 10.3.1 and to 10.4.3, characterised strictly and never overstated. In 10.3.1: name the standard-form families (NEC, FIDIC, JCT and their civil-law counterparts) as **privately published model forms whose effect derives entirely from being incorporated into a contract, not from any legal status**, and note ISO 44001 as voluntary guidance on collaborative business relationships. In 10.4.3: name the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights and the OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises and its Due Diligence Guidance as **non-binding international instruments** that supply the method (risk-tiered diligence, remediation-first response) but impose no obligations of themselves, expressly distinguishing them from the national due-diligence legislation the section already discusses; and ISO 20400 as **voluntary guidance, not a certifiable requirement**, on sustainable procurement. Apply the same treatment to the other unanchored domains — for Domain 15, the ISO 21500-series portfolio and programme standards as voluntary; for Domain 16, a records-management and a service-transition reference.

Location: domain-11-stakeholders-communication-influence.md — "11.1.2 Assessment — influence, interest, attitude and consent risk", "11.A.2 The stakeholder register as a decaying asset", "Toolkit 11.T.1 — Stakeholder register and engagement allocation sheet"
Issue: Toolkit 11.T.1 specifies a register row containing a **named individual**, a subjective **attitude assessment "with the evidence"**, an influence score, a consent-risk judgement, and a relationship map of "who they follow, who follows them". That is a file of personal data holding recorded opinions about identified people, and Domain 11 supplies no treatment of it: no statement that it is personal data, no lawful basis or owner, no access restriction, no retention or deletion point, and no caveat that in many jurisdictions the individuals concerned may be entitled to see what is held about them — which changes how attitude entries should be written. 11.A.2 treats register decay purely as an accuracy problem (30.6 % annual role-holder turnover) and prescribes refresh, never deletion of the departed holder's assessment. The omission is internally inconsistent: the domain's own KA 11.3 AI section already states the correct principle — "an assessment of a colleague's motives generated by a tool and stored in a project record is an employment and dignity problem regardless of its accuracy" — but applies it only to AI-generated content, not to the human-authored register the toolkit tells the reader to build.
Proposed correction: Add a paragraph to 11.1.2, "What the register is, as a record", establishing that a register naming individuals with attitude and influence assessments is personal data held by the organisation; that it needs a stated owner and access list rather than open circulation; that attitude must be recorded as an **observed position with its source** ("objected to the interface scope in the 14 March minute") rather than as a characterisation of the person; that entries for departed role holders are deleted rather than archived at the refresh in 11.A.2; that the register carries a deletion point at project closure; and that data-protection obligations, including any right of the individual to see what is held, apply on their own terms in their own territories and should be settled with whoever holds data-protection accountability in the organisation — this being illustrative of the discipline, not a statement of any jurisdiction's law. Add "access list", "deletion point" and "basis of the attitude entry (observed act and source)" to Toolkit 11.T.1, and cross-reference Domain 14 KA 14.4.4 and Domain 16 KA 16.4.4.

Location: domain-12-leadership-teams-behaviour.md — "12.4.3 Ethical leadership and the leader's own conduct"
Issue: The section handles the common cases well — report the forecast you believe in writing, state the date you can commit to, stop where the work can hurt someone — but every path terminates at the same place: "then letting the accountable person decide with the information". It never addresses what a professional does when the accountable person, having been told in writing, directs the misstatement anyway, or proceeds despite a stated safety objection. Missing entirely: the dissent record (what it must contain, where it is filed, who else receives a copy so it cannot be removed by the person it concerns); the escalation route beyond the accountable person — next governance tier, independent assurance or internal audit, then the board or its audit/risk committee; the point at which a leader must decline to sign an acceptance, readiness certificate or final account they do not believe; and any acknowledgement that protected-disclosure regimes exist, differ substantially by jurisdiction, and carry conditions. The section's own closing observation — that ethical failure is "an accumulation of small deferrals" — describes precisely the failure a route of last resort exists to prevent, and the domain elsewhere shows it can handle jurisdictional sensitivity well (12.3.4 on performance management is a model of it). This is professional obligation asserted without a mechanism.
Proposed correction: Add a subsection, "When the decision goes the other way", stating: the leader records a **dissent** — the fact stated, the date it was stated, to whom, the decision taken, and the risk the leader believes remains — filed in the decision record under Domain 3 KA 3.3.4 with a copy to a party other than the decision-maker; the leader does not sign an acceptance, readiness certificate or account they do not believe, and says in writing why; where the matter is a safety or harm risk the obligation to escalate beyond the accountable person is absolute and the route runs to the next governance tier, then to independent assurance, then to the board or its audit committee. Add a neutral closing note, expressly not legal advice: that many jurisdictions operate protected-disclosure regimes whose scope, conditions and protections differ materially, that the organisation's own policy and its legal function should be engaged before any external step, and that nothing here states the position in any jurisdiction.

Location: domain-14-digital-data-responsible-ai.md — "14.4.3 Human accountability and the AI use register" and "14.A.2 Drift, revalidation and the lifecycle of a model"
Issue: The word "escalation" does not occur anywhere in Domain 14. The AI use register is a strong preventive instrument — accountable person, consequence per escaped error, verification tier, prohibited adjacent uses — but the domain never states what a professional must DO once an AI output that was relied on in a recorded decision is later found to be materially wrong, or once differential error (14.4.2) is detected in a deployed system. Missing: who must be told, within what period; which decisions taken on the defective output are reopened and by whose authority; whether the register entry is suspended and the use stopped pending re-measurement; whether an affected person, counterparty, insurer or supervisory body is notified; and who authorises resumption. 14.A.2 supplies revalidation *triggers* but treats them as measurement hygiene, not as an incident with an accountable route — its only lifecycle actions are retirement and retention. The result is an AI-governance domain with a complete control set and no failure path, which is exactly the "governance asserted but not operationalised" pattern: 14.4.3 requires an accountable person for every output but never says what that accountability obliges them to do when the output fails.
Proposed correction: Add a short subsection at the end of 14.4.3, "When a relied-upon output turns out to be wrong", stating the obligation as a sequence: stop the use and suspend the register entry; identify every recorded decision that cited the output (which the register's "decision informed" column makes possible); notify the accountable person and the decision-maker in writing on the day it is known, applying Domain 11 KA 11.2.3's escalation-grade message; reopen decisions above a stated materiality threshold with the same authority that took them; record whether an affected person, counterparty or supervisory body must be told and on whose determination; and require a named authority to re-measure p and q before the use resumes. Add two columns to the register and to Toolkit 14.T.1: "Failure route — who is notified and within what period" and "Decisions to reopen on failure". Add to 14.A.3: "Every register entry names a failure route, and every AI-informed decision can be found from the output that informed it."

Location: domain-15-programmes-portfolios-enterprise.md — "15.2.1 The portfolio benefits register and the four double counts" and "Toolkit 15.T.3 — Portfolio benefits bridge" (with domain-16 "16.4.1 The benefits measurement plan")
Issue: The portfolio benefits register is defined with a measure, baseline, receiving-organisation owner and contributing components — but with no **cashable / non-cashable** classification, and the domain never uses the word. Worked example 15.2.1 then applies an investment committee's **four-year simple payback rule** to a benefit stream that visibly mixes fund types: released clinician time from chasing paper referrals, released administrative posts valued at 42,000 each, "improved decision-making", and pharmacy stock savings. Payback compares a cash outlay against a cash return; applying it to released capacity treats a benefit that never leaves anyone's budget as if it repaid the 4,880,000. The whole professional conclusion of the example — that reconciliation moves payback from 3.5188 to 4.3129 years and flips the committee's decision — rests on a denominator whose composition is never disclosed. The book plainly knows the distinction: KA 15.3.4 correctly excludes the 364,800 of eliminations from the enterprise PMO's value case because "eliminating a double count creates no value", and Domain 16's healthcare industry variation notes benefits there are "overwhelmingly capacity rather than cash". Domain 16 KA 16.4.1's required elements of a benefits measurement plan omit the classification too, so the gap survives to closeout. The governance consequence is concrete: an approval granted on a payback test that finance cannot honour, with no named authority having been asked whether the saving is budget-removable.
Proposed correction: Add a mandatory classification to the register in 15.2.1 — cashable (budget-removable, with the budget line named), capacity-released, cost-avoidance, or non-financial — and state the decision right: the **finance owner of the affected budget**, not the portfolio board or the delivering component, confirms cashability in writing, and an unconfirmed cashable claim is recorded as capacity-released until it is. Restate the worked example's payback test as applied to the cashable stream with the capacity stream reported alongside, or state explicitly which of the five components' benefits are cashable and that the rule is being applied to a mixed stream by the committee's own convention. Add the classification column and the finance-owner confirmation count to Toolkit 15.T.3's integrity checks, and add the same field to the required elements of Domain 16 KA 16.4.1.

Location: domain-06-evm-eac.md — "Knowledge Area 6.3 — Forecasting with EVM: the EAC family" (and domain-07-contracts-commercial.md "Knowledge Area 7.2 — Contract management")
Issue: "AI in this KA" coverage across Domains 1–7 is uneven and is thinnest at the highest-risk Knowledge Areas, which sits awkwardly against 00-conventions.md §1, where the 20 % AI weighting is stated to be carried in part by "the 'AI in this domain/KA' sections embedded in every non-AI chapter". Domain 1 has a block in all five KAs; Domain 4 has three of four. But Domain 6 — the EVM flagship — has only one, and it sits in KA 6.4 (limitations), so KA 6.3, described in its own heading as "the heart of the domain" and the home of predictive EAC (the single most consequential AI application in project controls, per 13.5.3), carries none. Domain 7 likewise has one block, in KA 7.5, so KA 7.2 — claims and variations, where contract-analytics AI is most used and where a missed notice window or a hallucinated clause is most damaging (13.5.7b describes exactly this workflow) — carries none. Domain 2 has none in KA 2.1 or 2.4; Domain 3 none in 3.1–3.3; Domain 5 none in 5.1 or 5.3.
Proposed correction: Add an "AI in this KA" block to KA 6.3 (predictive EAC: value in trend detection and driver attribution; limits — the model cannot see the critical path or the cause of a variance, cannot select among methods (a)–(d), and cannot own a forecast defended to a board; verification via the TCPI check of 6.2.3 and the CPI-stability test of 6.A.5) and to KA 7.2 (contract analytics: value in coverage across many contracts; limits — extraction is not entitlement, a model must not be relied on to confirm that a notice window is open or that a clause is a condition precedent; verification by reading the cited clause against the executed contract). Then audit the remaining KAs in Domains 2, 3 and 5 for the same gap so the AI surface is even rather than opportunistic.

Location: domain-08-pm-lifecycle.md — 8.5.1 "Contract and project closure" and Toolkit 8.T.2 "Project closure checklist"
Issue: Record retention is repeatedly required and never specified. 8.5.1 lists "archiving records" as a closure activity; Toolkit 8.T.2 has the line "Records archived — cost ledger, change log, contemporaneous records, schedule history". Neither states for how long, to whose custody the archive passes once the project team disbands, in what form (retrievable and readable, not a dead file share), or what drives the period — the contract's limitation period and defects-liability period, statutory accounting and tax retention requirements, funder or regulator conditions, and open or foreseeable disputes — nor that these periods differ by jurisdiction and contract. A search across all six domains for a retention period returns nothing. The omission has direct consequences elsewhere in the book: Domain 10 Advanced 10.A.6 states that contemporaneous updates "are the raw material of every credible method" of delay analysis, and Domain 9 KA 9.6.4 rests assurance on archived Sprint evidence, but neither is supported by a rule that keeps those records alive long enough to be used.
Proposed correction: Expand the 8.5.1 archiving sentence and the 8.T.2 checklist line into a retention requirement: records are retained for a defined period set by the longest of the contract's limitation and defects-liability periods, statutory accounting/tax retention, and any funder, regulator or audit condition — with any records subject to a live or foreseeable dispute held until it is resolved; the archive passes to a named custodian in the permanent organisation (typically the PMO or records function) with retrieval tested, not assumed; and the period is stated in the closure plan rather than assumed. Add the jurisdictional caveat that statutory retention periods and limitation periods differ by jurisdiction and contract form. Cross-reference from Domain 10 Advanced 10.A.6 and Domain 9 KA 9.6.4.

Location: domain-01-foundations.md — "Toolkit 1.T.3 — Conflicts and AI-use register" (same defect across Toolkits 3.T.1, 4.T.4, 5.T.1, 6.T.3, 7.T.3, 8.T.1)
Issue: Every domain ends in adoption-ready registers, and none of them states a retention expectation. Toolkit 1.T.3 is the clearest case: it captures conflicts (relationship, parties affected, disclosure date, handling, review date) and AI use (tool, environment, data classification, verification steps, named verifier, disclosure status) and closes with "One register, one owner, standing agenda item" — but never says how long the register is kept, in what form, or who holds it after the engagement ends. These are precisely the records a professional would need years later to show that a conflict was disclosed at the time or that an AI-assisted figure was verified before it entered a negotiating position, which is the defence Worked example 1.3.3 spends a page establishing the economic case for. The same silence runs through the assumption register (3.T.1), the hurdle-rate reconciliation sheet (4.T.4), the bankability condition register (5.T.1), the revenue stress and counterparty pack (7.T.3) and the contingency basis note (8.T.1). The audit brief lists record-retention expectations as a required element; the corpus supplies none.
Proposed correction: Add a standing retention line to the toolkit preamble that already appears in each domain ("Adoption-ready artefacts; adapt headings to your organisation, then keep them stable") — e.g. "and set a retention period against each: these registers are the evidence that a decision was taken properly, so they are retained at least as long as the obligation they support, in a form that opens without the tool that created them, with a named custodian after the engagement ends." Then add an explicit retention/custodian row to Toolkit 1.T.3 in particular, since conflicts and AI-use records are the ones most often needed after the people involved have moved on. Note in the preamble that the applicable minimum periods are set by the organisation's own policy and by jurisdiction-specific statutory and limitation requirements, which the book does not state.

Location: domain-03-time-value-of-money.md — "3.3.4 Day-count conventions"
Issue: The section is otherwise exemplary — it prices the actual/360 uplift at 8.33 basis points, ties it to coverage, and correctly concludes that "conventions are contractual, not conventional" and that a model needs a date-driven interest calculation. But the convention table is incomplete in a way that leaves the date-driven calculation unspecifiable. Three omissions: (a) actual/actual is absent, which is the convention most bond and some multilateral facilities use and the one for which the leap-year discussion is actually the defining case; (b) 30/360 is given as a single rule when the common variants differ on month-end and 31st-day treatment and produce different interest on the same period, so "the facility says 30/360" is not yet an implementable instruction; (c) most consequentially, business-day conventions — following, modified following, and whether period end dates roll — are not mentioned at all, even though they change the actual number of days in the accrual period and the actual payment date, and therefore change every figure the section computes. A modeller who implements the day-count basis correctly and ignores the rolling convention still builds the wrong schedule, and the toolkit (3.T.1) that records conventions per instrument does not list it.
Proposed correction: Add actual/actual to the table with its typical home. Add a short paragraph after the table: name that 30/360 has variants that differ on month-end treatment, so the register records the variant and not just "30/360"; and name business-day conventions (following, modified following, preceding) and end-of-month rolling as separate inputs that determine the accrual period's day count and the payment date, with the point that a schedule can implement the day-count basis correctly and still be wrong by a period if the rolling convention is not implemented. Add both — day-count variant and business-day/rolling convention — as explicit rows in Toolkit 3.T.1 ("TVM assumption register"). Keep the existing counsel caution, which already covers the case where the facility is silent or ambiguous.

Location: domain-08-cost-schedule-contingency.md — "8.1.2 Estimate classes and the contingency a range implies"
Issue: The estimate-class ladder is correctly and carefully disclaimed — "it reproduces no other body's classification and should not be read as one" — but it names no owning body at all, saying only that "professional estimating bodies and large owner organisations publish classification frameworks of their own". That leaves the book inconsistent with its own stated policy in two places. STANDARDS.md's "What this register does not contain" says that where a body of practice is discussed — and it names cost-estimate classification as its example — "the reader is pointed to the owning body rather than given a paraphrase of its text"; here the reader is pointed to nobody. And registries/EXTERNAL_AUTHORITIES.md already carries verified entries for AACE International Recommended Practice 17R-97 and 18R-97 (EXT-065, EXT-066, both confirmed current, revised 7 August 2020), used elsewhere in the programme, with the note that no accuracy ranges or class tables are reproduced — which is exactly the treatment 8.1.2 already applies. The practical consequence is that a practitioner cannot map the PCI illustrative ladder onto the classification their own organisation actually uses, which is the whole point of a class-based contingency argument in a room with an estimator.
Proposed correction: Name the anchor for identification only, in the same form Domain 5 already uses successfully for the Equator Principles: add a sentence such as "The best-known published frameworks are AACE International's Recommended Practices on cost-estimate classification — voluntary professional guidance, not a standard and not a regulatory requirement, and the property of their publisher; they are named here so a reader can locate the framework their own organisation uses, and nothing from them is reproduced or summarised below." Keep the existing disclaimer sentence verbatim. Add the reference to pfl-ai/STANDARDS.md under a "cost management" grouping and link the D8 usage to EXT-065/EXT-066 in registries/EXTERNAL_AUTHORITIES.md.

Location: domain-12-contracts-transaction-structure.md — KA 12.3, §12.3.2 "Guarantee sufficiency: cap times credit quality" and Toolkit 12.T.2
Issue: Related-party governance is stated once in the assigned range — in §12.1.4, for the O&M contract only ("where the O&M contractor is an affiliate of the sponsor … the conflict must be disclosed and the agreement tested on arm's-length terms") — and is not carried to the places where the arithmetic depends on it. §12.3.2 prices a parent company guarantee at a 0.70 probability of payment and derives a 1.4286× equivalence, correctly noting that the probability is correlated with the event that triggers the call, but not noting the sponsor-identity correlation: where the guarantor sits in the same group as the sponsor providing the equity commitment and the cost-overrun undertaking, the same balance sheet is being counted twice across Domain 12's security package, Domain 9's contingent equity and Domain 14's in-balance cash call. Sponsor-affiliate EPC contracting is at least as common as affiliate O&M, yet §12.1.1–12.1.3 apply no arm's-length test to the cap stack, and Toolkit 12.T.2 has no related-party column and no disclosure or approval field.
Proposed correction: Add to §12.3.2's "three further disciplines": where the guarantor is in the sponsor's group, identify every other obligation resting on the same balance sheet (equity commitment, contingent equity, cost-overrun undertaking, any other project's guarantees) and state the aggregate, because the risk-adjusted cover and the equity support are not independent. Extend the §12.1.4 arm's-length rule to the EPC contract and the security package with one sentence in §12.1.1. Add two columns to Toolkit 12.T.2 — "related party (Y/N) and relationship" and "other group obligations resting on the same obligor" — and a field recording the disclosure made and the body that approved the related-party arrangement.

Location: domain-15-operations-performance-restructuring.md — KA 15.4, §15.4.5 "Handback and the residual obligation"
Issue: The handback topic is developed purely as a funding-profile optimisation (697,844.05 vs 297,725.66 annual contribution; the indifference-rate invariant at the discount rate; "below the discount rate, sponsors rationally defer and grantors rationally insist"). Two professional dimensions are missing. First, accounting: the residual obligation is normally recognised as a provision that unwinds through the income statement over the concession, and remeasurement on the condition survey can move reported profit and net assets — which matters where any covenant or distribution test has an accounting basis, and which the discounted-cash-flow framing entirely omits. Second, and more consequentially, the section presents the funding profile as negotiable in every case, when in several sectors the security for decommissioning or handback is set by a regulator or a statutory régime rather than by the grantor's preference, with prescribed instruments, prescribed timing and no scope to defer — so the text's central behavioural conclusion is stated more broadly than it holds. Neither point is caveated, and "jurisdiction" appears nowhere in the topic.
Proposed correction: Add a short closing paragraph to §15.4.5: (a) state that the residual obligation is normally provided for in the accounts, that the provision unwinds over the concession and is remeasured on survey, and that the reporting framework and its interaction with any accounting-based covenant must be confirmed with the reporting accountants — flagging that the framework is jurisdiction- and standard-specific; (b) qualify the deferral conclusion by noting that in regulated sectors the form, timing and quantum of decommissioning or handback security may be prescribed by statute or by a regulator and is not a negotiable funding profile, so the professional first step is to establish whether the obligation is contractual, regulatory or both; and (c) name the owner and approver of the recommended "reserve plus handback bond or parent guarantee" structure, and require the condition-survey date and estimate vintage to be a standing board-reported item rather than something discovered two to five years before expiry.

Location: domain-08-risk-uncertainty-resilience.md — "8.3.1 Selecting and costing responses"
Issue: The response families are presented as an economic menu ranked by total expected cost, with two stated limits: a response must reduce EMV by more than it costs, and existential impact is not managed by EMV. Neither limit covers the case where the risk engages a legal duty. The text never states that a statutory, regulatory or safety duty cannot be transferred — a contract or insurance policy can move the financial consequence, in part and subject to enforceability, but the duty and the accountability remain — nor that acceptance is not an available response where realisation would breach such a duty, however favourable the arithmetic. The transfer discussion is admirably careful about counterparty risk and enforceability (it sends the recovery percentage to counsel) but frames the whole question as recoverability of money. Since Domain 1's proportionate-verification example expressly rules out expected-value reasoning where a statutory duty or licence is engaged, the risk domain's response-selection rule should carry the same boundary, and its absence leaves the two treatments inconsistent.
Proposed correction: Add a third governing rule after "Impact governs survivability even at low probability", worded to match 1.4.3's existing formulation: where a statutory duty, an operating licence or a safety obligation is engaged, the duty is not transferable and acceptance is not an available response — insurance and contract terms move money, not accountability, and only to the extent the wording and the jurisdiction allow. State the practical consequence for the worked example: rows whose realisation would breach such a duty are removed from the EMV comparison before it is run, and the comparison then prices only how the duty is met, not whether. Flag the corresponding register field (a mandatory/duty-engaged flag, mirroring Domain 5's non-prioritisable regulatory class and Domain 1's "mandatory — not an expected-value decision" marking) and add it to Toolkit 8.T.1.

Location: domain-08-risk-uncertainty-resilience.md — "Why this domain exists" / "Knowledge Area 8.1 — Threats, opportunities and identification" (systemic across Domains 2–8)
Issue: External-standard anchoring is effectively absent outside Domain 1. Across the eight domains reviewed, the only external references are the ISO family named once in Domain 1's historical-shifts table and AACE's cost-estimate classification in Domain 7.1.1. The risk domain never references ISO 31000 despite Domain 1 naming it as the risk anchor; the governance domain never references ISO 21505 despite Domain 1 naming it as the governance anchor; the integration domain never references ISO 21502. The consequence is that a practitioner reading the KA that actually treats the subject is never told which external authority governs it or where to go for the requirements, and the standards named in Domain 1 read as historical decoration rather than as live anchors. The book's own STANDARDS.md is careful and well-drafted, which makes the disconnection between register and manuscript the defect rather than the characterisation.
Proposed correction: Add a single anchor line to each domain opener ("Why this domain exists"), in the form the volume already uses: name the relevant external document, characterise it accurately as voluntary guidance describing practice rather than a requirement or legislation, state that it is named and not reproduced, and point the reader to the publisher for the current edition — e.g. ISO 31000 for Domain 8, ISO 21505 for Domain 3, ISO 21502 for Domain 4, ISO 21504 for the portfolio material of Domain 2, AACE's Total Cost Management framework for Domain 7 (already present at 7.1.1, so promote it to the opener). Update the "Discussed in" column of STANDARDS.md accordingly so the register and the manuscript agree.

Location: domain-09-quality-assurance-improvement.md — "9.3.1 The acceptance decision and nonconformance disposition" (cumulative-effect test)
Issue: The cumulative-effect test is asserted but not operationalised: "related concessions aggregating above a threshold within a period require the authority appropriate to the aggregate". The text never says who sets the threshold, at what level or on what basis, over what period concessions are aggregated, what constitutes "related", who monitors the running total, or what happens when it is breached — Toolkit 9.T.2 asks for "cumulative concession value against threshold" as a monthly count without ever defining the threshold's source. The word "escalate" appears twice in the whole domain, neither time in the acceptance chain. Also unstated: that in approval-regime sectors (aerospace, rail signalling, medical devices, pressure and nuclear systems) a concession or repair may require notification to, or acceptance by, a certifying body or regulator before the item is used — an obligation the delivery organisation cannot discharge internally, and which the domain's disposition table, whose authority column stops at "design authority", currently implies away.
Proposed correction: In 9.3.1, state who sets the concession threshold (the sponsor or design authority at baseline, not the delivery team, recorded in the quality management plan of 9.1.3), the aggregation period, the test for relatedness, the named owner of the running total, and what breach triggers — suspension of further concessions in that class pending a decision by the authority appropriate to the aggregate, taken through Domain 3's escalation machinery. Add a sentence to the disposition table's surrounding text: where an approval regime applies, a repair, concession or regrade may additionally require notification to or acceptance by the certifying body or regulator before use, that obligation sits outside the project's authority, and the applicable requirement differs by sector and jurisdiction.

Location: domain-12-leadership-teams-behaviour.md — "Toolkit 12.T.3 — Difficult-conversation preparation and record"
Issue: The toolkit instructs the reader to create, within 24 hours of every performance, conduct or expectation conversation, a written record containing dated observations about a named individual's work, the other party's account, and what was agreed — and then says nothing about the record as a record. There is no custodian, no access list, no retention period, no statement that the individual receives a copy (the toolkit asks for "their confirmation that the record is accurate" without saying they hold one), and no distinction between the leader's working note and a document that may later be produced in a formal process. The closing sentence correctly routes formal-consequence cases to HR and legal and defers to the jurisdiction's requirements, but that is about the *conversation*, not the *file*. Given that 12.3.4 already establishes that fair process is jurisdiction-specific and 12.4.1's AI treatment already warns that individual telemetry inference is "restricted or unlawful in many jurisdictions", the domain has the sensitivity elsewhere and loses it in the artefact practitioners will actually adopt.
Proposed correction: Add a closing block to Toolkit 12.T.3: named custodian; access limited to the leader, their manager and HR; a copy provided to the individual; a retention period taken from the organisation's employment-records policy rather than set by the project, with disposal at the end of it; and a note that where the record may feed a formal process the HR and legal functions own its retention and access, and the applicable requirements differ by jurisdiction — nothing here stating the position in any of them.

Location: domain-13-agile-adaptive-hybrid.md — "13.1.2 Product ownership as a decision right"
Issue: The section defines the product owner as "the single individual accountable for the order of the backlog — for deciding what is built next, and therefore what is not built next — within a value envelope set by the sponsor", and bounds the right in exactly one way: a monetary envelope of USD 25,000 per change, above which the decision escalates. It never states the other boundary — that certain items are non-deferrable regardless of their computed delay-cost density, because they are safety, regulatory, statutory, contractual or security-remediation obligations rather than value propositions. In a health exemplar this matters: 13.1.3 orders the backlog by priced delay-cost density, and nothing in the KA prevents a clinical-safety or information-governance item from being sequenced downward because its computed density is low. The domain's Industry variations paragraph for healthcare gets the governance half right (clinical sign-off sits with clinical authority, and those classes cannot be written-resolved) but that is a statement about who approves a decision class, not about what the product owner's ordering right may not reach — and it appears 1,200 lines after the decision right is defined.
Proposed correction: Add a fifth paragraph to "What the role must be able to do" — or a short "What the ordering right does not reach" — stating that the product owner orders discretionary value, and that items carrying a safety, regulatory, statutory, contractual or security obligation are **constraints on the order, not candidates within it**: they are scheduled to their required date by the accountable authority for that obligation, they are excluded from the delay-cost-density ranking of 13.1.3, and an owner who deprioritises one has exceeded the right rather than exercised it. Cross-reference Domain 3's decision classes and the healthcare industry variation.
